hops.title: A fruit fly gene that stands in for its mouse cousin
hops.text: In flies, atonal builds the chordotonal organs: stretch receptors in the body wall and joints, and antennal hearing organs. Its mouse relative Atoh1, then called Math1, is needed for inner-ear hair cells, skin touch cells, cerebellar granule neurons and gut secretory cells. At the time, fly atonal had no known gut role, though later work suggested a role in adult gut enteroendocrine cells. In 2000, researchers put mouse Math1 into atonal-null flies and partly restored the stretch organs. In 2002, Vincent Wang, Hugo Bellen, Huda Zoghbi and colleagues gave fly atonal to Math1-null mice. The mice grew no insect parts; the fly gene fully rescued them.

hops.title: Blocking a vessel Delta gives tumours more vessels and less growth
hops.text: Many tumours support their growth by growing new blood vessels. In 2006, teams at Regeneron and Genentech blocked Dll4, the Delta that vessel-lining cells use to activate Notch in their neighbours. The mouse tumours responded with markedly more vessels, more sprouts and more branches, and yet they grew less. The new vessels carried blood poorly, and the tumours became more short of oxygen. Work on the mouse retina published weeks later offered an explanation for the extra tumour sprouts: sprouting retinal vessel cells use Dll4 through Notch1 to stop neighbours from also becoming branch-leading tip cells. Without that "not you", far too many cells lead.

image.caption: Without Dll4 telling neighbours "not you", too many vessel cells sprout, and the tangle carries blood poorly.

hops.title: Birds regrow hearing cells, and mice can be pushed to
hops.text: Adult humans do not naturally replace hearing cells lost to loud noise. In 1988 Jeffrey Corwin and Douglas Cotanche showed that chickens replace hair cells destroyed by noise, apparently from supporting cells that divide. Later bird work found that Notch limits how many supporting cells convert: block it, Atoh1 activity rises, and extra hair cells appear. In 2013 Kunio Mizutari, Albert Edge and colleagues treated noise-deafened four-week-old mice with a gamma-secretase inhibitor, a drug that blocks Notch among other targets. Some supporting cells became new hair cells and hearing partly recovered, though the authors cautioned it may work only soon after the damage.

audio.title: A fly gene in a mouse, chickens that regrow hearing, and a slower human clock
audio.transcript:
Proneural genes and Notch were worked out in fruit flies, so it is fair to ask whether any of it matters for animals like us. Here are three true stories where the same parts turn up somewhere unexpected.

The first is a gene swap between an insect and a mammal. In flies, the proneural gene atonal builds the chordotonal organs, the stretch receptors in the body wall and joints, and the hearing organs in the antennae. Mice have a relative called Atoh one, first named Math one. It is needed for hair cells in the inner ear, touch cells in the skin, granule neurons in the cerebellum, and secretory cells in the gut. Back when the teams swapped the genes, fly atonal had no known gut role, though later work suggested a role in hormone-secreting cells of the adult fly gut. So in two thousand, researchers put mouse Math one into flies lacking atonal, and it partly restored their stretch organs. In two thousand two, Vincent Wang, Hugo Bellen, Huda Zoghbi and colleagues tried the reverse and gave fly atonal to mice lacking Math one. The mice did not sprout insect parts. The fly gene fully rescued them. The two versions can do much of the same work, and the surrounding tissue helps shape what develops.

The second story stays in the inner ear. Adult humans do not naturally replace hearing cells lost to loud noise. In nineteen eighty-eight, Jeffrey Corwin and Douglas Cotanche showed that chickens replace hair cells destroyed by noise, apparently from neighbouring supporting cells that divide. Later work in birds found that Notch acts as a limit on that repair. Block Notch, and Atoh one activity rises and more supporting cells become hair cells. Adult mammals do not naturally replace hearing cells lost from the cochlea after noise damage. But in two thousand thirteen, Kunio Mizutari, Albert Edge and colleagues treated noise-deafened four-week-old mice with a gamma-secretase inhibitor, a drug that blocks Notch among other targets. Atoh one levels rose in the cochlea, some supporting cells became new hair cells, and the mice got some of their hearing back. The recovery was partial, and the authors cautioned that it may work only soon after the damage. Later work in cultured neonatal mouse cochleae found that supporting cells lose most of their hair-cell production in response to Notch blockade within the first week after birth, and raised the possibility of a Notch-independent effect in mature mice. Still, Mizutari and colleagues showed in two thousand thirteen that a gamma-secretase inhibitor could push some surviving supporting cells toward a hair-cell fate in noise-injured young mice.

The third story is about timing. Hes one is part of the brake in this lesson. Its protein turns down its own gene, the RNA and protein fade quickly, and with a delay before new protein appears, levels rise and fall every couple of hours in stimulated cultured cells. A close relative, HES seven, runs the same kind of clock in the embryo, where it times the body segments. In twenty twenty, Mitsuhiro Matsuda, Miki Ebisuya and colleagues grew this clock in a dish from mouse and from human stem cells. The mouse clock ticked every two to three hours. The human clock took five to six. The obvious guess was a difference in the gene itself, yet swapping the human HES seven gene region into mouse cells slowed the mouse clock by only twenty to thirty minutes, far short of the roughly two-hundred-minute gap between species. Instead, human cells simply ran the steps more slowly: the protein was broken down more slowly, and the delays in making it were longer. Same loop, same parts, slower chemistry.
